questions.q: Per this lesson, what question does a load balancer answer?
options: Which healthy instance of the same service should handle this request?
Should this request be authenticated before it reaches any instance?
What rate limit applies to this client?
How should the request body be transformed before reaching the backend?
questions.explain: A load balancer spreads traffic across multiple instances of the same running service -- that's its one job.

questions.q: What does the API gateway handle that a load balancer does not, according to this lesson?
options: Restarting a crashed container instance
Routing, auth, and rate limiting before a request reaches application code
Building the container image from a Dockerfile
Assigning CPU and memory to each instance
questions.explain: The gateway handles cross-cutting concerns -- routing, auth, rate limiting, request shaping -- before your application code ever runs.

questions.q: In the Amazon API Gateway console walkthrough, what does the proxy resource pattern (/{proxy+}) do?
options: It blocks all traffic to a path by default
It automatically load-balances across every backend instance
It forwards everything under a path to the backend, which does its own internal routing
It encrypts every request body before forwarding it
questions.explain: Instead of defining every endpoint by hand, a proxy resource forwards the whole path to the backend and lets the backend route internally -- a common pattern for AI apps.

questions.q: Where do rate and burst limits live, per this lesson's stage screen example?
options: Inside the application's own source code
In the Dockerfile's CMD instruction
In a separate billing dashboard, unrelated to the deploy
On the stage itself, enforced at the gateway before a request reaches the backend
questions.explain: The stage screen that produces the invoke URL is the same screen where rate and burst limits are set -- enforcement happens at the gateway, not in app code.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say gateway-level rate limiting matters more for an AI app than a typical CRUD API?
options: AI apps never need authentication, so rate limiting is the only protection available
AI inference calls are comparatively slow and expensive, so a careless client loop can run up a large bill or cause an outage fast
CRUD APIs cannot be deployed behind a gateway at all
AI apps don't use HTTPS, so gateways handle encryption instead
questions.explain: A plain CRUD API's requests are small and cheap; an AI app's prompt payloads and inference calls are larger and far more expensive per request, so unmetered traffic is a bigger risk.
